but revealing itself in the very essence of the will, the will is from God, and this same God in the will, introduces himself into the hardening <note>original: *verstokkinge*; refers to the spiritual state of being calloused or closed off to grace, like the "hardening of Pharaoh's heart."</note>, just as he introduces himself into hell in darkness and pain; it is to be understood in the same way regarding the kingdom of grace.

56. God wills nothing in man but good, in the kingdom of his grace; when the free will enters into grace, then God, through that grace, wills the good within the will.

57. But if one were to say that man cannot turn his will toward the good—that is, toward grace—such a claim is without foundation. For grace stands in the <term>Abyss</term> <note>original: *afgrond*; in Böhme's thought, the "Abyss" is the deep, underlying spiritual foundation present in all things, even those that seem godless.</note> of the Creature, even in all godless Men; and the will needs to do nothing else than to stand still from its false activity, and so it begins to sink into its own will, into the abyss.

58. For that which stands still, stands still with the eternal One, and becomes one single being with the One, for it enters into its "nothingness." A false will must certainly stand still from its unrighteous works for the sake of worldly laws, out of fear of punishment; why then not also for the sake of God's commandment? If a man can obey his worldly lord and stand still at a specific place, wherever the lord wants him to be, why can he not do so for God? For the "ability" is given to him immediately, provided he only joins his will to the act of standing still.

59. But the reason the entire false, godless will does not stand still and turn to grace is this: it is already a "born thistle." <note>Böhme uses the metaphor of a thistle to describe a nature that is inherently prickly and resistant; just as a thistle and a lily both receive the same sunlight, their inner natures determine whether they produce a flower or a thorn.</note> Grace lies too deep within, and the wrath of God is too strong in its nature. Grace draws the person and shows him his falsehood, yet he despises grace and works like a thistle in the power of the Sun. To God, this is a "good scent" even unto the damnation of death in hell, so that grace may be distinguished from the false will.

60. But the conclusions of <term>Reason</term> <note>original: *vernuft*; refers to human intellectual logic that tries to understand God without spiritual illumination.</note>, which say that God in himself—insofar as he is named "God"—has decreed that a portion of humanity (indeed, the greatest multitude) shall and must be damned, and that he hardens them out of a preconceived will of his own: this is false. It has no ground in scripture, nor in the light of Nature, if one considers the scripture rightly and does not look at it blindly.

61. For in God, insofar as he is named "God," there is no preconceived plan nor any beginning will. He is himself the will of the <term>Unground</term> <note>original: *ongrond*; Böhme’s central term for the absolute, bottomless depth of the divine reality that exists before any specific form, thought, or "will" emerged.</note>, being a single unity, and he wills nothing in himself but the good. Therefore, he is himself that same willing good; for the good that he wills is the birth of his power, namely, his Son.

<meta>This page continues Chapter 61, moving from the internal spiritual state of the individual to a broader theological defense of free will against strict predestination. Jacob Böhme uses the story of Jacob and Esau to explain how God’s grace is universal, but its effect depends on the "ground" or nature of the soul that receives it.</meta>

### How Jacob and Esau come together. Chapter 61.

62. God, in Himself, wills to reveal nothing other than His own goodness, which is what He is. This could not happen unless the one and only power of goodness, through its "out-breathing" into the desire for Nature and for "separability"—that is, into the <term>perceptions</term> <note>original: *scients*; a term Böhme uses to describe the various "knowledges" or "powers of differentiation" that allow the one Divine light to be perceived as many things.</note>—introduced itself. For if the Good remained a single unity, there would be no knowledge or awareness.

63. Yet the Good—which is God in Himself—does not make itself evil or divided. Rather, it is the <term>perceptions</term>, being the <term>fiat</term> <note>Latin: "let it be"; the creative command or desire.</note> or the desire for separation, that introduce themselves into Nature and the Creature. From these perceptions, both evil and good arise; they do not come from God or exist within God in His triune essence.

64. For in God there is no <term>decree</term> <note>original: *decret*; a reference to the theological idea of predestination, where God decides someone's fate beforehand.</note>. If there were a deliberation or a plan there, then there would also have to be a cause for that plan, and a cause for that cause in turn. Then something would have to exist before God or after God, about which He would have to deliberate.

65. But He Himself is the <term>Unground</term> <note>original: *ongrond*; Böhme’s term for the "bottomless" or "unoriginated" depth of God that exists before all created things.</note> and the One. He is a single will, which is He Himself, and that will is solely good. For a single thing cannot be against itself; it is only *one* and has nothing to struggle against.

66. Therefore, it is a foolishness of human reason when it speaks of the "compulsion of necessity" and does not understand the <term>Great Mystery</term> <note>original: *mysterium Magnum*; the hidden, chaotic, yet fertile ground of all reality.</note>. Or when it says: God, by His own purpose, does not wish to move the evil will (which He has hardened) through His grace.

67. I present to this blind reason the image of a thistle. The sun moves upon the thistle the whole day and gives it light and power, yet it remains a thistle. So it is with the godless will: the Divine Sun shines upon it the whole day of its life, but its inner ground is a <term>Thistle-Essence</term> <note>original: *Distel-Ens*.</note>.

68. Otherwise, if God hardened him by a fixed purpose, then divine justice would have no basis for judgment within him. For he who does what he must do is simply following his Lord’s will. However, since the godless nature does not please God—as seen in <note>original: *Jesa: 5*; Isaiah 5.</note>—the evil arises from the root, and stays in the root, of the "knowledge" coming from the ground of nature to the creature, and through chance. For this reason, God has revealed His will and given the Law and the Gospel; that is, He has revealed His punishment and His grace, so that a Day of Separation may be held with justice, and so that no creature can excuse itself.

### How Jacob and Esau come together. Chapter

62. God, in Himself, wills nothing but His own goodness, which He Himself reveals. Such a revelation could not occur unless the singular good power, through its "out-breathing" into the desire for Nature and into differentiation—that is, into the <term>scients<note>From the Latin 'scientia' (knowledge); here, it refers to the branching out of the unified divine will into multiple specific desires or forms of knowledge.</note></term>—introduced itself. For if the Good remained a single unity, there would be no working knowledge.

63. Yet the Good, being God in Himself, does not make itself evil or divisible; rather, it is the <term>scients</term>. It is the <term>fiat</term> <note>Latin: "let it be," the creative command or formative power.</note>, or the desire for divisibility, that introduces itself into Nature and the Created Being. It is from these <term>scients</term> that evil and good arise, and not out of God or in God within His Trinity.

64. For there is no "decree" there <note>referring to the internal life of the Trinity</note>: if there were a predetermined counsel within it, there would also have to be a cause for that counsel, and then a cause for that cause in turn; there would have to be something existing before God or after God about which He deliberated.

65. But He is Himself the <term>Unground</term> <note>original: 'ongrond'; a central concept in this theology referring to the "Abyss" or the absolute Divine state before creation and before the distinction of light/dark or good/evil.</note> and the **One**. He is a single unity which is Himself, and He alone is good. A single thing cannot be its own opponent, for it is but **one** and it has nothing to struggle against.

66. Therefore, it is a folly of human reason to speak of compulsion or inevitability, for reason does not understand the <term>Mysterium Magnum</term> <note>Latin: "The Great Mystery," the hidden foundation of the universe.</note>. Reason claims: "God, by His own purpose, does not wish to move the evil will (which He has hardened) through grace."

67. I present to this blind reason the image of a thistle: the sun moves the thistle and gives it light and power all day long, yet it remains a thistle. So it is with the godless will; the Divine Sun shines upon it all day long, but its inner foundation is a **Thistle-Essence**.

68. Otherwise, if God hardened a person by His own purpose, then Divine Righteousness would have no basis for judgment within them. For he who does what he *must* do lives according to his Lord’s will. However, because the Divine being "does not please God" <note>original: 'Jeſa: 5'; a reference to Isaiah 5, where the vineyard produces wild grapes despite the gardener's care.</note>, the evil arises from the root—and in the root—out of the "knowledge" from the foundation of nature within the Creature, and through chance. Because of this, God has revealed His will and given the Gospel to the world; that is, He has revealed His punishment and grace so that a "day of separation" may be held with justice, and no creature can excuse itself.

2. Leah, Jacob’s wife, bore Jacob six sons, being half the tribes of Israel, and from her came Judah, being the root of David, from whom Christ was manifested according to our humanity. 4. Just as a harlot shines outwardly and adorns herself, wishing to be called a chaste virgin, so also would this adorned Christendom wish to be called holy, but her heart would do nothing else but dally with fleshly lust.

13. Learn to know her for what she is; she gives Shechem cause for fornication, for she runs out of her house and seeks lovers. Look at her pride; tear the earrings <note>original: *oorfpanfels*</note> from her neck with which she flaunts herself, so she shall no longer boast so. Demand her idols from her, bury them as Jacob did, build the altar within yourselves, and lead your children to the sacrifice. Do not command them to fight for Dinah, but let Dinah take the man who slept with her, or you shall fight in vain for her virginity; for it is public knowledge before all nations that she has committed harlotry.

14. Note what has been said to you: it is time, for her shame can no longer be covered, because she has given birth to the child of harlotry. Do you not see it, and do you not recognize the harlot and the child? If not, you are blind.

15. She sits in high human honor and blesses herself; this is the one with whom you commit adultery, forsaking your God and His altar, Jesus Christ, within you. Have mercy upon yourselves and behold your misery: how this harlot is seated in the place of God's Altar in your souls, and has taken over your body and soul. She rides upon you as if you were an animal; she leads you by her bands, and you do not see it; you say, "this is how it should be." O, you wicked beast full of the pride of your harlot! How the Lord shall cast you down along with the harlot, as is seen in the Revelation <note>A reference to the Whore of Babylon in the biblical Book of Revelation</note>.

### How God Commanded Jacob to Depart for Bethel, Cap. 6.

16. The Spirit here further points out an excellently beautiful figure <note>The author uses "figure" to mean a prophetic symbol or "type" that foreshadows a future spiritual reality</note> of how God revealed Himself to Jacob after he had built the altar at Bethel and named the place **El-Bethel** <note>original Hebrew: "God of the House of God"</note>, it being an angelic dwelling. There, God interacted with Jacob in an angelic form, as the high tongue <note>The "high tongue" likely refers to the sacred Hebrew language or a divinely inspired mode of speech</note> indicates; how God spoke with him in an angelic form in a vision—that is, in the angelic form of the future humanity of Christ. He told him that he would no longer be called Jacob, but **Israel**, which is to say a great tree, or a multitude of nations <note>The author provides a mystical interpretation of the name "Israel" here, linking it to growth and the gathering of peoples</note>; who would be so blessed by God that he would possess all these lands and become so great that even Kings would come from his loins. Here, the Spirit pointed toward the future Kingdom of Israel and of Christ, showing how it would come to pass.

17. And when the Lord had spoken with Jacob, Jacob set up a stone sign <note>A pillar or monument</note> at that same place, which points to the Temple of Christ, as well as the Temple in Jerusalem as a prefigure of Christ, and likewise the Christian Church among the Christians. It shows how one should build a place and a sign from the Word of the Lord where people would come together to proclaim the wonders of the great God, and call upon Him there, and offer up the drink-offering of prayer.

18. And the Spirit says further: thus God ascended from him when He had spoken with him. That is, once He had appeared to him in a visible form in the image of Christ, He hid Himself again in the Royal place, from which He would later reveal Himself and make Himself visible in His seed <term>seed: descendants or biological lineage</term> through this figure in humanity.

19. And Jacob called this place **Bethel**, which means a humbling of the Godhead into humanity <note>While "Bethel" literally means "House of God," the author interprets it here through the lens of the Incarnation—God coming down to dwell with man</note>, where the Divine Altar is made manifest and where one offers praise to God. Thus, through Jacob's Bethel, the Spirit points toward the future **Bethlehem**, where Christ was to be born as a man. Just as this place, Bethel, is frequently mentioned by the patriarchs, it all points together toward the future Bethlehem. There, the true Altar, Christ, would be built and raised up, upon which Jacob, his fathers, and his children have offered in faith and prefigure. Meanwhile, God ascended from them in a visible image until the appointed time when this Altar was raised in Bethlehem with the birth of Christ.

20. And the Spirit in Moses speaks immediately after this in a figure that is entirely dark <note>meaning "obscure" or "mysterious"</note>, saying: "and they journeyed from Bethel." Here he indicates the departure from the prefigure of Christ; how one would go out from this symbolic figure toward the actual birth of Christ. He says that while they were still a stadium <note>A unit of distance; an ancient Greek measurement</note> away from **Ephrath**, Rachel gave birth, and she had a hard time in her labor.

### Chapter 63. And how Rachel gave birth to Benjamin.

21. This distance <note>The original Dutch uses "stadie," referring to a stadium or a specific measure of distance, here used allegorically to represent a stage of spiritual progress</note> indicates the time that still remains before the Altar of Christ; specifically, that Adam had gone out one distance from the Altar of God—that is, out of the Spiritual world into the earthly one. Here, Rachel—representing human Nature—now comes close to giving birth to the patriarch Benjamin, namely a Christian, so that in this birth, the old Adam must also die and perish, just as Rachel died when she gave birth to Benjamin.

22. This Benjamin indicates that when we erect the Altar of God within ourselves, so that Christ dwells in us, then Benjamin is born—that is, our "last man" <note>The "last man" refers to the final, perfected state of humanity in Christ, contrasting with the "first man," Adam</note>. Then the old Mother dies, she who gave birth to the kingdom of Nature in man, and that new Spiritual man is revealed.

23. This Benjamin is first born after Jacob's departure from Mesopotamia, once the Spirit of God had prefigured the suffering and victory of Christ through the figures of Esau and Jacob in their meeting. It was also a figure <note>A "figure" or "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic prophecy of the New Testament</note> of the Apostle Matthias, who was chosen as an Apostle only after the Ascension of Christ and after the completion of His suffering, taking the place of Judas.

24. In the same way, this is the figure of how a person must first enter into the suffering and death of Christ, and that the Altar, Christ, must be erected within him beforehand, before the human Nature is born out of Christ. For Judas—representing the old Adam—must first hang himself in his falsehood and betrayal, with remorse for the sins committed, and despair of his own power and die; only then is Benjamin born, being the new creature in the Spirit of Christ, and Matthias—that is, the first-created Adam—is chosen as an Apostle.

25. For Matthias was already born before the suffering of Christ, and he was with Christ, but he only became an Apostle when Christ had died to sin within him and Judas had hanged himself. So too is the Adam-like man, who shall become an Apostle or Christian, already born beforehand, before Christ suffers in him; but Christ must first rise from death within him, and Judas—being the wild serpent—must first hang his evil will in the death of Christ and die. Only then does Adam's man first become a Christian. The "historical man" <note>The author distinguishes between an "historical" Christian (one who only knows the facts of the Bible) and a "spiritual" Christian (one who experiences Christ internally)</note> does not become a Christian through an "imputed grace" where Judas still lives under the Purple Cloak of Christ <note>A critique of those who claim salvation through Christ's merits while continuing to live in sin</note>—just as Babylon <note>The author uses "Babel" or Babylon to represent the corrupt, confused state of the institutional church</note> plays very cunningly under the cover of the maidenhood of her daughter Dinah, so that the beautiful little daughter may carry out her harlotry and sleep and dally softly and sweetly with her lover, (Judas).

They would be very good and useful and would not need to be rejected, if only Reuben would cease his harlotry, with which he defiles her; if her servants were renewed and did not appoint themselves—without the anointing of the Holy Spirit—as ministers of this concubine of God <note>The "concubine" here likely refers to the external, visible church structure, which is meant to serve God but is often treated as a secondary or worldly thing by corrupt leaders.</note>, as happens now solely for the sake of temporary honor and pleasure. These [ministers] are as useful to the churches as a fifth wheel on a wagon; except that even without them, they travel on their wagon with five wheels, while the fifth hangs in the air, and with their strife, they journey into the abyss of hell.

47. The stone house of the church has in itself no greater holiness than other houses, for it is built of stones like other houses, and God is no more powerful within it than in all other houses. But the congregation that enters and meets there, and unites themselves there with their prayers into a single body in Christ—of which the church is an example—that congregation has the holy temple of Jesus Christ within itself.

48. Their song of praise is the cradle of the infant Jesus Christ, where the infant Jesus is rocked with a courageous voice in the hearts of men, and not in the understanding of the church, which is **Mute**.

49. Her ministers are no more than any other men, but the power which is exercised in the anointing of the Holy Spirit, that [power] has the authority in the offering and is the key.

50. Whoever wishes to enter the church worthily must bring the temple of Jesus Christ within himself into it, or at least have such an intention that he wishes to carry the same out in his heart; otherwise, with his going in and out, he has practiced nothing but a spiritual, hypocritical harlotry, and is no holier when he leaves. 51. Through our understanding of this figure <note>The "figure" refers to a biblical person or event acting as a symbol for a deeper spiritual truth.</note>, we wish to point out that a Christian must not look upon the outward appearance of the Churches. Instead, he must realize that the Church is merely an image or example of Christ. One is not a Christian simply by entering into the example and professing oneself to it. Rather, a true Christian is one who enters into the incarnation, the suffering, and the death of Christ. Such a person allows their hypocrisy <note>original: "Huychelerye"</note> to die away in the death of Christ and rises from that death with a new will and in obedience. According to their inward ground, they live and exist in Christ; they themselves become the temple of Christ, in which Christ works with His power, thereby killing sin within the flesh. Such a person is a Christian in Christ and may rightly enter into the "example" <note>The visible, physical church building or community.</note> and practice their Christianity within it; such a person shall hear God’s word and preserve it in their heart.

52. And even if it were the case that a sheep-bell rang out the name of God in its sound, Christ would still preach within the person themselves. But the dead cannot wake another from death, nor can one blind man show the way to another; otherwise, they both fall into the ditch, as Christ says.

53. Furthermore, the spirit of Moses presents in his figures the death of the Father Isaac, saying: Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, in the city named Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac lived as strangers. And Isaac became one hundred and eighty years old; he declined and died and was gathered to his people. This is a figure of how the children of Christ, in their pilgrimage, are nothing other than strange children <note>Meaning "foreigners" or "sojourners" who do not belong to the worldly kingdom.</note> and possess nothing of their own in the world. Finally, they all return together to their first Father who created them, just as Jacob returned to his father at the end. Thus, in this pilgrimage within this earthly Church, we are nothing other than house-guests and foreign children, for we must finally enter into our true Fatherland, which is the Angelic Church of Christ.

Chapter 64. On the 36th and 37th Chapters of Genesis concerning Joseph. 191

# THE 64th CHAPTER.

## Concerning the 36th and 37th Chapters of Genesis, being the beginning of the entire beautiful figure <note>The author uses "figure" to mean a symbolic representation or "type" where Old Testament characters prefigure New Testament truths.</note> of Joseph the son of Jacob, and what is to be understood by it.

<margin>1.</margin>
The 36th chapter is the genealogy of the mighty tribe of Esau, showing how God gave him great riches and many children and grandchildren. The Spirit provides a great record and describes his children and grandchildren, showing how great princes came from them who possessed the glory of this world. Meanwhile, regarding Jacob, the Spirit says nothing of any present worldly glory, but speaks only of the future kingdom in the figure of Christ.

<margin>2.</margin>
In this we see clearly how Esau stands as a figure of the kingdom of nature, and how the glory of nature fell to his lot. He became a great prince and fathered many princely tribes. We see how God blessed him and made him great, and how the Holy Spirit recorded his lineage with particular diligence. This indicates that we must learn to rightly understand the figure of Jacob and Esau, and not rush so blindly to condemn Esau to the abyss as happens all too often. For we see how his father Isaac appointed him a rich dwelling on earth, as God wished to give him much temporal blessing; however, his figure, representing Adam’s nature, had to perish so that Christ could rise in him. This was so that from the name E-S-A-U, the "S-A-U" <note>This is a mystical linguistic play. The author suggests that by removing the "SAU" (associated with the fallen, animalistic nature), only the "E" remains.</note> would be brought to naught, and he would remain in the "E," that is, as an Angel <note>original: "Engel"</note>, a transformation that Christ, in the figure of Jacob, wished to help him achieve.

<margin>3.</margin>
The Spirit also gives Esau a name through Moses, calling him *Edom*, who had his dwelling in the mountains of Seir. There is a hidden meaning beneath this, for in the "high tongue" <term>The "high tongue" refers to a mystical or primordial language—often called the *Lingua Adamica*—believed to reveal the inner essence of things through their names.</term>, Edom indicates a "red-colored one"—specifically one who would be dyed red through the red blood of Jesus Christ within his hard, mountainous nature.

<margin>4.</margin>
And the Spirit says further that those two brothers separated from one another. This signifies that the natural Adam and Esau would separate their will from Jacob, that is, from Christ; for a natural self-will shall not behold God. It also indicates how the

33. ->Of Judah and Tamar, Chapter 65<-

# CHAPTER 65.

### *Regarding Judah and Tamar, a hidden Figure of Adam and Christ, wherein the New Rebirth is excellently prefigured, based on the 38th Chapter of Genesis:*

1. When one considers the history of Joseph according to outward human reason, reason says: "Why does the history of Joseph in the Bible not continue sequentially, since it actually happened in that order? Why does Moses place the figure of Judah and Tamar in between?" However, if we look at and reflect upon this history of Judah and Tamar, and then Joseph’s figure with a right understanding, we see that the Holy Spirit has placed them in this order with great diligence and total correctness.

2. For Joseph is the image of a Christian—how a Christian stands before God and before the world in this world, and how he is placed in the process and in the figure of Christ. But the history of Judah and Tamar is now a figure of how a Christian, according to humanity, must arise out of Adam’s image in the Kingdom of Nature—that is, out of the first Adamic image—and how that same Adamic image is evil and must die; that it is killed by the wrath of God, and how nevertheless the first true image must exist. It shows that a Christian, according to human nature and property, is nothing other than that same Adamic image and no stranger; and how Christ reveals Himself in this Adamic evil image and kills the evil, yet a Christian outwardly clings to it in this time; the spirit <note>The author often refers to the "spirit" as the guiding divine inspiration behind the biblical text.</note> prefigures <note>original: *præfigureert*</note> this here very powerfully.

3. For here we see a powerful figure in Judah, in whom the <term>Line of Christ</term> <note>original: *Linea Christi*. This refers to the genealogical succession leading to the birth of Jesus.</note> stood according to the order of generations, from which Christ would become manifest. This indicates that even the children of God, in their corrupt Nature, perform nothing but harlotry before God, and that their marital state is nothing but a harlotry and a stained, beast-like <note>original: "veehagtige," referring to the lower, animalistic nature of fallen humanity.</note> state before God, and there is entirely nothing good nor any purity before God in it. Therefore the Line of the Covenant revealed itself in this harlotry of *Judah* and *Tamar*, indicating that *Christ* would come in this Line of the Covenant and enter into the midst of this harlotry, and that he would crush the head of the false harlot-desire and Earthly serpent, and purify our Fleshly, unclean, beast-like conception with his heavenly virginal seed, and change it back into the paradisical image in himself.

40. Since the Line of the Covenant lay within Judah for its revelation and propagation, and because Israel—according to the <term>Adamist Nature</term><note>The "Adamist nature" refers to the fallen, sinful state of humanity inherited from Adam.</note>—was also impure, God placed His Covenant of Grace within the first propagation from the tribe of Israel in such a <term>Figure</term><note>A "Figure" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of Christ or spiritual truths.</note>. 41. We see such a Figure also with the Royal Prophet David and Bathsheba, upon whom the Line of the Covenant pressed forward with Solomon. And even though David had her husband Uriah killed and committed a falsehood so that he might take Bathsheba as a wife—which was an abomination and a great sin before God in human nature—the Spirit also had its Figure there with David. Since God renewed His Covenant of Grace from Christ with him, God placed the Line of His Covenant into David’s unrighteousness with the very same woman whom he had wrongly drawn to himself in harlotry by murdering her lawful husband. This shows that the whole of human essence is vain and evil before God, and that He Himself wills to come to the aid of our sins and impurity with His grace. He introduces His grace into our sins to kill those very sins with grace. Therefore, God presents this image in David for reconciliation in view of the future coming of Christ. When Christ entered into these Figures, He took the sin of all people upon Himself and purified the harlotry of Judah and Tamar, as well as that of David and Bathsheba, and even Adam and Eve. He led them back to Himself in the true marriage bed, just as He did with Judah and Tamar, and David and Bathsheba, in whom the Line of the Covenant became manifest despite their evil intentions.

42. For here the old proverb was fulfilled: "Where God builds a church, the devil builds a chapel next to it."<note>original: "daar God een kerk bouwd, daar bouwt de duyvel een kapel neven." Yet the Church of God always resisted the chapel of the devil.

# Of Judah and Tamar, Chapter 6

...even the debtor himself: indicating that *Christ* also placed himself in the judgment of the world, within this **Line of the covenant**. He acted as a righteous one who wished to separate right from wrong and condemn the harlotry and idolatry of the world. Yet, in contrast, we see in this **Figure** <note>In this mystical tradition, a "figure" is a person or event in the Old Testament that serves as a symbolic blueprint or "type" for spiritual truths revealed later in Christ.</note> how *Tamar* presented the pledge—namely the ring, the cord, and the staff—before the heavy judgment of *Judah*. By doing so, she overturned the judgment *Judah* had pronounced and stilled his wrath, so that he was moved to have mercy on her and grant her justice.

53. This figure also stood before God in the internal depths of *Judah* and *Tamar*, and not just in *Adam* and *Eve*. For *Adam* had immersed himself in fleshly, earthly desires; through his **imagination** <note>To these writers, "imagination" is not just fantasy, but a creative spiritual force that "shapes" the soul into the image of what it desires.</note>, he had committed "harlotry" within the animal nature and forgotten the heavenly, magical nature of Divine honor. Because of this, the "Heavenly Woman" <note>This refers to the "Sophia" or Divine Wisdom, the spiritual counterpart of the soul that was lost during the Fall of Man.</note> died within him, and in her place, the earthly, beast-like nature awakened. It was with this animal nature that he now practiced harlotry. God placed this very condition within *Adam* himself as a judgment, intending to condemn *Adam* to death, just as God's righteousness had already condemned him.

54. But the re-incorporated *Eve* within the **covenant of grace**—meaning the "seed of the woman" from the essence of the heavenly world—stepped before the strict judgment of God and spoke to God's righteousness: "Behold, I have become pregnant by the man to whom these things belong." That is to say: "Behold, I have taken *Adam's* soul, spirit, and body as a pledge; I am mingling with him again and am married to him." I have taken the Father's Nature (which was awakened in Wrath) into my love, and I am now pregnant with human nature and shall give birth to the **God-man**.

55. And when the Father's **property** <note>The "properties" are the various qualities of God's being, such as Love, Wrath, Light, or Fire.</note> within the soul's nature recognized that the Father had sown Himself back into grace—namely in the **new Eve** within the covenant—the Wrath of the Father within the soul spoke to this new *Eve*: "You are more righteous than I." For I caused the impurity of *Adam*, so that he became earthly and committed harlotry before me. And I have not given *Shelah* <note>Shelah was Judah's youngest son, whom he withheld from Tamar. Here, he symbolizes the Law of Moses.</note> to the new *Eve* as a husband; that is, I have not given the Word for the new **rebirth** through the Law or in the Law. Therefore *Tamar* (the new *Eve*) dallied with *Judah* and his children during the time of the Law for the sake of the soulful and human nature. She left *Shelah* (the Law) standing aside in this figure, and the grace of the new *Eve* in the covenant has continually mingled with God's children. This is seen in the Saints and especially in the Prophets, who outwardly lived under the Law and performed its duties, yet all the while mingled with the new *Eve* in grace.

->*The most beautiful Figure <term>Figure: In this context, a "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament person or event that serves as a symbolic prophecy of Christ or the spiritual life of a believer.</term> of Joseph; how he was sold to Potiphar; what occurred with Joseph regarding Chastity and Godliness.*<-

And from that time on, when he had set him over his house and all his goods, the Lord blessed the house of the Egyptian for Joseph’s sake; and there was a singular blessing of the Lord in everything he had under Joseph’s hands, and he did not trouble himself with anything while he had him, except for what he ate and drank. That is, when Christ becomes manifest in him, he is no longer his own, to do whatever he wishes; nor does he possess anything in this world as his own property that he can say with truth: "it is mine, I am it," or "I have it, it is my own; I may do with it what my flesh and self-will desires, I may use it for my own honor and pleasure, so that I may be exalted in the world through it." No, a right Christian has none of that in his power.

# How Joseph was sold to Potiphar. Chapter 66.

...obedience of faith, bought through the blood of Christ for 30 silver pieces <note>The author draws a numerological connection between the 30 pieces of silver paid for Christ (Matthew 26:15) and the 20 pieces paid for Joseph (Genesis 37:28).</note>; of these, his Lord Christ has given him Joseph’s 20 silver pieces and placed him over them as a Steward, so that he may trade with them until he also makes 30 silver pieces from them; these he must carry within himself as a mark of his Lord Christ, as a treasure of his Christianity.

4. But since his Lord Christ was betrayed and sold to death for 30 silver pieces, and Joseph was sold by his brothers for 20 silver pieces to be a bondservant <note>original: "Lyf eygen knegt," literally a servant whose body is owned; a slave.</note>, in both of these stands the *Figure* of a Christian. Namely, when Christ becomes manifest in a person, he shows that person the 30 silver pieces for which he was sold to Suffering and Death. This Suffering and Death the person takes upon himself, in which the Figure of the 30 silver pieces—just as Christ was betrayed and sold—stands engraved. There the person becomes a Christian, in the Suffering and Death of Christ; he stands in Christ’s Figure and loses the right to his Natural self-will, as well as the kingdom of this world.

5. For according to his inner Spiritual man, he dies to this world in the death of Christ, and according to that same inner Man, he is no longer in this World, but in Christ, in God—that is, in the kingdom of God. As it is written: *the kingdom of God is within you* <note>Luke 17:21</note>; likewise, *test whether Christ has gained a form in you*; likewise, *you are a Temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you*; likewise, *you are servants of Christ, and shall eat the flesh of the Son of Man, so he remains in you and you in him, and without him you have no Life* <note>John 6:53-56</note>. Just as a herb and grass, as well as all earthly things, have no life, growth, nor effect in themselves without the power of the sun, so also man, without the Divine Sun—who reveals Himself through Christ in his Christian—has no life or salvation outside of Christ within himself.

6. 7. ->### How Joseph was sold to Potiphar. Chapter 9.<-

...in that same state, he could neither be God’s servant nor a helper to his fellow branches <note>In this mystical context, "branches" refers to fellow human beings, as in the vine and the branches (John 15).</note>, nor give them his strength, will, and being. Instead, he said, "Mine," meaning "it is my own; I want to keep it for myself alone, and in me it shall rest." He wished only to fill his own body and, through it, be highly esteemed and a lord over his miserable, languishing branches; yet he falsely withdrew from them the sap <note>A metaphor for the vital resources or spiritual grace needed to sustain life.</note> with which they should strengthen their lives, and dragged it into a sense of "mine." God takes this violence away from the Christian and makes him once again a sustainer of his brother—that is, a householder for his Lord. He lets him remain in the temporal goods he possessed, so far as he possesses them by **natural right** with justice and truth, and makes him into a "Joseph" within those goods.

10. This "Joseph" then does not say: "That village, city, land, principality, kingdom, and empire are mine; likewise, that house, field, money, goods, wife, woman, and children are mine." He has appointed me as ruler and householder therein, so that I may employ it for the purpose He desires. I must nourish my children and His—namely, the needy—therewith, and must be their sustainer. I must also share with them my strength and understanding from the Divine gift, and therewith instruct, serve, and govern them in goodness. Just as God governs me with His Spirit, so must I, who am His **official** <term>original: "Amptman," a steward or deputy acting on behalf of a superior</term> in this world, govern with my understanding and other fellow members in such power, and nourish them; for all the goods over which I rule are not mine, but God’s and theirs; yet I may do for them just as God does for me."

11. To such a person, God gives Joseph’s understanding and wisdom, and through him governs the house of this world. In whatever state he may be, he sits there in the office of God, and is nothing other than a servant of the office of a sustainer of God's creatures. Where one takes such pleasure in oneself in such finery <note>original: "Ciragie" — refers to ornate decoration or jewelry</note>, and where people bestow great titles of honor upon one another—where the house is full of adorned harlots hiding under a chaste appearance—there the Devil is a cheerful guest, for it proceeds according to his own nature and will.

55. But if God sends a Joseph there, who gladly wishes to live and act according to the will of God, then it goes with him just as it did with Joseph, and with Daniel, whom they falsely brought to the lions' den, and Joseph into the dungeon; yet the Kingdom of the Devil is ultimately brought to shame, as seen with Joseph and Daniel.

56. Therefore, if anyone wishes to be a Joseph, and also wishes to sit in worldly offices and honors, he must do so with great earnestness and with the humility of his heart, and pray constantly and resist the Devil, so that the Devil does not come to dwell with him upon his seat of pride. If not, let him stay away from it, or he shall perish in such offices. If a "Joseph" is not armed with Christ—who has overcome the Devil—let him certainly leave the high offices untrodden, for the Devil will not tolerate him there since he is against him; he must practice being a true Joseph and Daniel, or he must possess the mind of the World if he wishes to rule the World.

57. For this World has two kinds of offices: namely, God’s office and Satan’s office. One is in God’s Love, the other in the wrath of God; that is, according to the nature of light and of darkness, which rule alongside and within one another in the nature of this World. And these are two Kingdoms: namely, one is the Kingdom of Christ, and the other is the Kingdom of Satan.

58. Therefore, if you are not armed and entirely surrendered to God—so that in times of need you can, like Joseph, abandon your coat, and with it your honor and goods, for the sake of righteousness and the will of God, and overcome the Devil with Divine power—then do not press yourself into any office unless you are orderly called to it. For only then do you stand either in Joseph’s seat or in the World’s seat.

59. In an office, you must serve either God or the Devil, for you cannot serve two masters at once; for <term>self-interest</term> <note>original: "eygenheid" — the state of being focused on one's own ego or possession</note> and <term>resignation</term> <note>original: "gelatenheid" — the mystical practice of yielding one's will to God (Gelassenheit)</note> are two different things.

63. In this final trial, man becomes the **image of God** once again, for all things become the same to him; he becomes equal with good fortune and misfortune, with **poverty** and **wealth**, with joy and sorrow, with light and darkness, with life and death—everything is one to him. He is to himself as a nothing, for in his will, he is dead to all things; he stands in the figure <note>The "figure" here refers to a symbolic or representative form</note> just as God is in everything and through everything, and yet is a "nothing" to everything, for it does not grasp Him. And yet, everything is made manifest through him, and he himself is everything; yet he has nothing, for the "something" is before him, in his understanding, also as a nothing because it does not grasp him. He is all things as if they were one, and yet he is the very life of all things. He is the "One," and yet also nothing and everything. A man also becomes thus according to his **resigned will** <term>resigned will</term> (original: *gelaten wille* – a spiritual state of total surrender or "letting go" of the ego): when he gives himself over entirely to God, his will falls back into the **unfathomable will** <term>unfathomable will</term> (original: *ongrondelijke wille* – the divine "Ungrund" or groundless source of all being) of God, from which he came in the beginning; he then stands in the form as an image of the unfathomable will of God, in which God dwells and wills.

64. For when the **Creature** <term>Creature</term> (the created human being) wills nothing more than what God wills through it, it is dead in its **selfhood** and stands again in the first image—that is, the state in which God formed it into a life. For what is the life of the creature? It is nothing other than a **spark** <note>original: *vonxken* – a mystical term for the divine essence or "seed" within the human soul</note> of the will of God; when that creature's will stands still, its life and will is God, who drives and governs it.

65. But that which wills and runs of its own accord separates itself from the whole will of God and leads itself into **selfhood**, in which there is no rest; for it must live in its own willing and running, and it is sheer **unrest**. For **unrest** is the life of the self-will: for when the will no longer wills itself, then nothing can torment it any longer. Its willing is its own life, but that which wills nothing else but what is in and with God—that is a life with God.

66. It is better to know nothing than to will for oneself; for that which knows nothing, its will perishes with the life of the creature, and its struggle has an end, and it has no more torment, as we may understand from the unreasoning creatures <note>i.e., animals, who do not suffer from the same ego-driven anxieties as humans</note>.

67. For the torment of all the damned is that they "will"—namely, they want **selfhood**—and in their will, they give birth to forms: namely, conflicting desires or opposition. Where the wills are in conflict, so that a single thing is manifest in many at once, in that very thing it is its own enemy. But if it is only "one" with the Eternal One, then no **enmity** can be in it, and there is no possibility for **enmity**.

68. Therefore, this is the last trial of man: when he stands still for God in all things, then a light becomes for him out of the darkness, and a life out of death;

Then he shall become more powerful within himself than the world and Hell are; for after he withstands all tests, they all finally become a thing of mockery.

2. # CHAPTER 68.

->*Concerning the dreams of King Pharaoh; how Joseph was taken from the prison-house, and was set before the King, and came to great honor.*<-

<margin>Gen: 41.</margin>
Moses says: and after two years Pharaoh had a dream; how he stood by the water, and saw seven beautiful fat cows coming up out of the water, and they went grazing in the meadow; after that he saw another seven cows coming up out of the water, which were ugly and thin, and they stood next to the cows on the river bank. And the thin and ugly ones ate up those same beautiful fat cows; then Pharaoh awoke. And he fell back into sleep, and he dreamed once more, and saw that seven full, thick ears of grain grew out of one stalk; after that he saw seven thin and scorched ears rise up, and the seven thin and scorched ears swallowed the seven thick and full ears. Then Pharaoh awoke and found that it was a dream; and when it became morning his spirit was troubled, and he sent forth and had all the soothsayers in Egypt called, and told them his dream; but there was no one who could explain the same to Pharaoh, etc.

2. These dreams were presented to Pharaoh by God; therefore the wise man <note>original: *Magus*</note> and the knower of nature could not explain them. For the natural magician <note>original: *Magus Naturalis* — a practitioner of "natural magic," which was considered a branch of science or natural philosophy dealing with the hidden properties of the physical world</note> only has power within Nature, and in what Nature is capable of forming in her operations. He cannot reach into or make known that which the word of God depicts figuratively; but the prophet has power therein to explain the same, for he is a Divine magician <note>original: *Magus*</note>, as Joseph was here.

### Chapter 68. And how Joseph was taken out of the prison.

3. Among the *Egyptians*, the <term>Magic art<note>original: "Magisch kunst." In this context, "Magic" refers not to sleight of hand, but to the deep study of the hidden forces of nature and the divine will.</note></term> was common; but when it was turned into an abuse and sorcery, it was rooted out. However, it remained among the *Pagans* until the Kingdom of *Christ*, when the *Divine Magic* arose. Then the *Natural Magic* perished among the *Christians*. In the beginning, it was indeed good that it perished, for the pagan faith was thereby extinguished, and the *Magic* images of *Nature*, which they honored as Gods, were thus rooted out from the hearts of men.

4. But when the faith of the *Christians* became common, other *Magi* arose, namely the sects within *Christendom*. These set themselves up as Gods in the place of the images of the pagan idols and practiced greater deceit than the pagans did with their magic images.

5. For the pagans looked toward the power and the working of the foundation of *Nature*, but these place themselves above the foundation of *Nature*, purely in a *Historical* faith, so that men should believe what they fabricate.

6. Just as today, the title of *Christendom* is full of such *Magicians*, where no *Natural* understanding—neither of God nor of *Nature*—remains with them anymore. Instead, there is only an empty chatter of a "super-natural Magic" foundation, in which they have set themselves up as idols and gods. They understand neither the *Divine* nor the *Natural Magic*; so that through them the world has become stone-blind. From this, strife and conflict have arisen in the faith, so that men speak much of faith, pulling it one way here and another way there, and making a heap of opinions. These are altogether worse than the pagan images which had their foundation in *Nature*; but these images have no foundation even in the super-natural *Divine* faith. They are mute *Idols*, and their servants are servants of <term>Baal<note>A reference to the Canaanite god Baal, used here as a biblical metaphor for false worship and idolatry.</note></term>.

7. And just as it was highly necessary and good that <term>Natural Magic<note>original: "Magia naturalis." The study of God's wisdom as revealed through the physical world.</note></term> fell among the *Christians* when the faith of *Christ* was made manifest, so it is today much more necessary that *Natural Magic* should once again be made manifest. This is so that the <term>"Title-Christendom"<note>A term for those who are Christian in name only, lacking true spiritual depth.</note></term> might have its self-made *Gods* revealed and recognized through *Nature*. Thus, men might recognize in nature the "spoken and formed word of God," as well as the new rebirth, and also the fall and corruption. By this means, the conflict and the fabricated "super-natural" gods might perish, so that one might finally learn to understand the Scriptures through *Nature*. 9. For the fathers of the first faith were not so blind to the Kingdom of Nature, but recognized in Nature that a hidden God exists, who has made Himself visible through the Word of His out-breathing and in the formation of the created world. They recognized God’s Word in the created world, which is much more necessary today, so that the gods of mere opinions might be brought to light and recognized for what they are, so that <unclear>that</unclear> one may see what faith is—that it is not just an opinion <unclear>or</unclear> a whim, but a Divine substance. 10. That the <term>Natural Magi<note>original: "Magi Naturales." These were scholars or "wise men" who sought to understand God by studying the physical laws of the universe, such as astronomy and physics.</note></term> could not interpret Pharaoh’s dreams happened because these dreams arose from the *Center* of Nature, which the pagan *Magi* did not understand. For their human foundation in understanding was only from the working and *form* of the stars and the elements; they did not understand the foundation of Eternal Nature, from which the nature of this world has its origin and in which it consists. But Pharaoh’s dreams had their origin in Eternal Nature and were placed into a visible image in the outward nature of time and in the outward *form* of the human being through the Word of God.

11. For the seven fat cows in the grass signify, in the internal foundation, the seven properties of Eternal Nature in the Holy Divine Being—that is, in the Kingdom of Heaven, where the Divine power is substantial. The seven thin, ugly, parched cows signify, in the internal foundation, the seven properties of Eternal Nature in the wrath of God—that is, in the kingdom of hunger and thirst, where Nature is without the Divine substance of God’s good power. The seven thick, full ears of grain, as well as the seven thin, scorched ears, also signify the same.

12. But that this dream appeared twice to Pharaoh points toward a figure; first, the foundation of Eternal Nature in its seven properties and what God wanted to show through them; second, because of the second appearance, it points toward the human foundation, which has its creaturely origin in its being from the seven properties. ->### Chapter 68. And how Joseph was brought out of prison.<-

Joseph’s counsel, after he had interpreted Pharaoh's dream, was as follows: he spoke to Pharaoh, saying that the King should look for a man of understanding and wisdom who might build grain-houses for Pharaoh. This would allow for a store of provisions to be gathered, so that there would be what is necessary during the time of famine. In a hidden way, the Spirit presents this in the <term>Figure</term> <note>In this context, a 'Figure' is a symbolic or allegorical person or event that points to a deeper spiritual reality.</note> of man: that a person must look for wise and God-fearing people who help gather the divine treasure and provision through wisdom, understanding, teaching, living, and prayer, so that a divine storehouse may be gathered through these means.

47. This is what God meant when He said He would do good to the God-fearing even unto the thousandth generation; that same provision shall last unto the thousandth generation.

# T H E 69th C H A P T E R.

*How this time of famine spread through all lands, and how Jacob sent his sons to Egypt for grain, and how they came before Joseph, and how he behaved toward them; what is to be understood by this.*

->Genesis 42.<-

<margin>1.</margin>This 42nd Chapter of Genesis, concerning Joseph and his brothers, is now a **figure** <note>In this context, a "figure" refers to a biblical "type" or allegory where historical events are seen as prefiguring spiritual or future realities.</note> of how God ultimately grants even his enemies to such a converted Christian—one who has had to enter into the <term>process of Christ</term> <note>The "process of Christ" is a mystical concept referring to the believer's inner journey of suffering, death to the old self, and rebirth, mirroring the life of Jesus.</note> and has now overcome. These enemies, through their persecution and false betrayal, were the ones who drove him into that very process. It shows how their sins are set before their eyes; how they are also led into anguish and distress; and how they are finally, out of pure grace, delivered from pain and punishment. It illustrates how God becomes so merciful to them because they repent; He not only remits the punishment but also endows them with His blessing, just as Joseph does here with his brothers.

<margin>2.</margin>But alongside this, it is also presented in this **figure** how God shows Himself so earnest against sins—just as Joseph here behaves toward his brothers. Yet, it is not God's actual intent to punish the repentant sinner most severely; rather, He sets Himself harshly against the soul within its conscience so that sins may awaken and be acknowledged. In this way, repentance becomes all the greater, so that the person, in such a terror of sin, might be humbled and depart entirely from sin, growing to hate it because he recognizes that sin contains such a terrible judgment within itself.
->The history reads thus.<-

<margin>3.</margin>But when Jacob heard that there was grain for sale in Egypt, he spoke to his sons, "Why do you look at one another for so long? See, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt; go down there and buy us grain, so that we may live and not die." Thus Joseph's ten brothers went down to buy grain in Egypt; but Benjamin, Joseph's brother, Jacob did not let go with them, for he said: "Lest a misfortune befall him."

<margin>4.</margin>This is now, first of all, a **figure**: that when a person finds himself in Divine Wrath, in such a <term>time of famine</term> <note>original: "dieren tyd," referring to a period of scarcity or high prices, used here as a metaphor for spiritual starvation.</note> where he lacks righteousness,

### How this time of famine spread through all lands, Chapter 69.

Just as Jacob did with his children during the time of famine, so the Father speaks within the conscience to the soul: "Why do you tarry so long and look around? Go down into repentance, where righteousness is to be obtained in the death of Christ. There, Christ gives righteousness for your sins, if only you heartily turn to him." In this way, the Father surrenders his will in the repentance and conversion of the sinner.

<margin>5.</margin> But Benjamin, Joseph’s brother—who represents the **humanity of Christ**—is not immediately given to the soul. He first gives the soul its sinful brothers; that is, he first gives it terror in its conscience and hides the comfort of his grace. He, being the true Benjamin, Joseph’s Brother, stands before the properties of sin and directs those very properties—in which the sins were committed—toward grace, so that one may buy such grain from Joseph, who is Christ.

<margin>6.</margin> The sinner must himself approach this and enter with earnestness into the suffering and death of Christ. They must allow their sin to die away before grace, within the prison of God’s wrath, and throw themselves upon mercy in Joseph—that is, in Christ's compassion. One must not merely stand outside and say, "Grace is to be found in Christ," and tickle and comfort oneself with grace. No, that does not refresh the poor soul. You must travel down into Egypt <note>In this mystical tradition, "Egypt" often symbolizes the physical world or the state of trial where the soul must go to find spiritual sustenance.</note> to your offended Brother, whom you, by your sins, have thrown into the pit within yourself. You must appear before his eyes in great humility, even if you do not recognize him at first, until he makes himself known to you in his compassion. There, in the powerful glory Christ obtained in his resurrection, you must buy grain for the poor soul so that it may live and not die, just as Jacob said to his children.

<margin>7.</margin> And Moses <note>original: "Moyſis"</note> says further: Thus the children of Israel came to buy grain among others who went with them; for there was famine in the land of Canaan also. Now, Joseph was a ruler in the land and sold grain to all the peoples of the land. When his brothers came to him, they fell down before him on the earth upon their faces. He looked at them and knew them, but he acted as a stranger toward them and spoke harshly to them, saying, "Where do you come from?" They said, "From the land of Canaan, to buy food." But although he knew them, they did not know him.

<margin>8.</margin> This is now the first state when the poor soul turns to Christ to fetch food from him. He sees the soul in its will, entirely in its essence—whether the free will has directed itself toward him. And if it has only just turned around, he knows it; yet, he first terrifies the <term>conscience</term> <note>original: "Conſcientie"</note> and behaves as a stranger, acting harshly toward the soul, just as he did toward the Canaanite woman <note>A reference to Matthew 15, where Jesus initially responds with silence and harsh-sounding words to a woman's plea to test her faith.</note>.

### Chapter 69. *And how Jacob sent his sons to Egypt.*

8. ...[to seek Him], and He hides His grace from the soul until it pours out its repentance and bows its face before Christ; and confesses all its guilt, and humbles itself completely to the pit of judgment, and yields itself into the Wrath and punishment of God—that is, into the dying of its <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: "selfheid"; refers to the ego or the selfish will that must "die" to allow for spiritual rebirth.</note>.

9. Then Christ looks into the soul and seizes her with the earnest bond of the Wrath of God; yet His love and grace only hide themselves within it. When the soul stands and calls to God, Christ speaks in the conscience: "Who are you? Look at yourself, and see if you are even worthy of me," just as Joseph did here when he said, "Who are you?" and acted as a stranger.

10. And Joseph remembered the dreams that he had dreamed of them, and spoke to them: "You are spies, and you have come to see where the land is open." This means: Christ remembers His mercy and His bitter suffering and death, and says to the soul: "You are a spy, and you come to me only wanting to see where the door of my grace is open; but that will not help you. You must go about it differently; you must first enter through the gate of my death and suffering. Otherwise, you are merely a spy, wanting to see where the door of my grace stands open so that you might cover yourself with it as a <term>cloak</term> <note>The author warns against using the idea of "grace" as a "cover-up" for continuing to sin without a true change of heart.</note>. For it thinks that if it comforts itself with the merits of Jesus Christ and believes in Christ (that He is the Son of God and has paid for sin), then it cannot be accused of being a spy of God or an unrighteous hypocrite. It believes it is indeed justified through the justification of Christ, since it believes that this was done for its benefit.

This does not avail for the soul; it must first enter into the Suffering and death of Christ, and this must be preceded by earnest repentance, and

# *How this time of famine spread through all lands,* Chapter 69

->The internal precious figure stands as follows.<-

14. When the soul thus approaches Christ and wishes to immediately "put on" His resurrection, the spirit of Christ speaks within the <term>essences</term> <note>original: "Essents" or "Essentien"; refers to the fundamental spiritual energies or "substance" of the soul's being.</note> of the soul: "That is what I have told you: your essences are, by the life of God, spies. This "youngest brother" is the true brother of Joseph, which is the <term>ingrafted line</term> <note>This refers to the "Seed of the Woman," the promise of grace "grafted" into human nature after the Fall to allow for eventual salvation.</note> of the covenant of grace in its heavenly essence (which became <term>faded</term> <note>original: "verblikt"; a mystical term meaning the divine light in the soul grew pale or lost its luster when Adam fell.</note> in Adam). This is the ingrafted covenant of grace that was established in Paradise; the soul's essences, with their internal foundation, must turn toward and into me. Otherwise, they come only as hypocrites and spies at the gate of grace.

15. This is rightly called "fetching the youngest brother." For that same ingrafted grace, which was given as a promise in Paradise, is the soul's "youngest brother." The soul hides and covers this brother with sin, and at the beginning of its repentance, leaves him "at home" by the life of God.

16. Therefore, the text of Moses says quite hiddenly that Joseph wanted to test them "by the life of Pharaoh." In the <term>Figure</term> <note>The spiritual or allegorical interpretation of the biblical story.</note>, this is called "by the life of God," by which this youngest son remained behind. A repentant person must bring this "youngest brother" to the gate of grace; otherwise, he must lie shut up and imprisoned for three days until he brings him, just like Joseph's brothers. That is to say, otherwise the <term>three principles</term> <note>A core concept in theosophy referring to the three realms within man: the dark fire-world of nature, the light-world of God's love, and the outer physical world.</note> in man must lie imprisoned in the Wrath of God for so long and cannot buy divine food, unless they have this youngest brother with them. They must bring the "gate" with them in which Christ rises from the death within man—in that same image of the heavenly world's essence which faded in Adam—so that He may have His dwelling-house there.

# Chapter 19. *And how Jacob sent his sons to Egypt.*

...turns to God, or if he completely and totally converts to God, and brings along this <term>ingrafted ground of grace</term> <note>referring to the "Precious Seed" or the spark of divine grace within the soul</note>, in which Christ wants to and must manifest Himself; if not, so speaks Joseph—that is, Christ—to the **essences** of the souls: "You are, by the life of God, nothing other than **spies**, and you only investigate the justification of man, and the Suffering and merit of Christ." God no longer wants to have it so; for He Himself tests the thoughts of men, and is Himself present in all things. The understanding is His; the knowledge of the kingdom of God is His; without Him you know nothing.

### Chapter 6. How this time of scarcity <note>The Dutch "dieren tydt" literally means "expensive time," referring to the famine in the Joseph story, which the author uses as an allegory for spiritual hunger.</note> has gone through all lands.

We find ourselves in want again precisely because, on that first journey, we did not bring our Benjamin with us—that is, the **innermost ground** <note>original: *allerinwendigsten grond*; refers to the deepest, most essential part of the soul where God dwells</note> of our being. Our will was not yet completely broken. If we had intended to remain until the very end in repentance and **Divine Resignation** <note>original: *God-delyke gelatenheyd*; a central mystical concept meaning the total surrender of one's own will to God's will</note>, as happened during that first repentance, then the Justice of God, acting in His Wrath, could not have taken a pledge from us, but would have had to set us entirely free.

19. This is what the story foreshadows: that the children of Jacob had to travel to Joseph in Egypt twice for food. It was only on the second time that Joseph revealed himself to them, and on the third time they brought their wives, children, and all their possessions along with their father. This means that when a person has consumed the first Divine food through sin, they must again hunger and suffer in their conscience. The conscience then presses and accuses them, just as a hungry stomach yearns for food; thus, the person remembers their first repentance and how grace was once granted to them.

20. But their innermost ground—being the bond of the **Wrath of God** <note>The stern, judgmental aspect of Divine nature that reacts against sin</note>—accuses and condemns them because they did not preserve that grace. It reviles them as a perjured and faithless person who tasted God’s grace—which was given out of pure mercy—and then ruined and lost it all for the sake of fleshly lusts. At that point, the person stands like one who is not worthy to look upon Heaven or to be supported by the Earth, because they squandered it all for base desires. They think of how they might turn back again to God’s grace, like the poor tax collector and sinner, or like the **Prodigal Son** <note>original: *verloren Soon den swyn-hoeder*; literally "the lost son, the swine-herder"</note>. Only then does it become a matter of **real earnestness** <note>original: *regten ernst*; a sincere, total commitment to spiritual transformation</note>. Then all the sons of Jacob journey together a second time to Egypt, in repentance, to buy heavenly grain. Meanwhile, the old Adam-like Jacob—representing the physical body—must remain at home in sorrow.

21. In this state of earnestness, Benjamin—the innermost ground—is finally taken along. Here, the "first will" <note>The superficial or ego-driven desire for salvation</note> is broken. The person no longer approaches Joseph as a "spy" <note>A reference to Joseph accusing his brothers of being spies; allegorically, seeking God with hidden or ulterior motives</note> as they did the first time. Instead, they come as truly earnest, hungry people—a hungry life that, with all its strength, hungers for the mercy of God and the food of Jesus Christ.

22. Now, the earnestness begins in trembling and fear. This is the true departure toward Heavenly food, where the conscience stands in anguish and the reason <unclear>fails...</unclear>

# Chapter 70. Returning again to Egypt to Jacob. #

In this, the Spirit portrays in the Figure how the Christian church—whenever she finds herself in such sorrow and spiritual famine, and is now on the path of repentance—must bring such good fruits before God: namely hope, faith, and Divine trust. Not wild fruits—namely greed, self-lust, and hypocrisy—but a resolve toward truth, righteousness, chastity, love, and gentleness.

35. In this way, the **old man** <term>old man: a biblical term referring to the unregenerate human nature or the self-centered ego that must be "put off" to follow Christ</term> must make a resolution that he will walk in such a will toward Joseph, that is, toward Christ. Only then does he surrender all his sons upon this pilgrim’s path, and says: "Now I am bereaved of all my sons; I no longer hold anything in luxurious fleshly desire; I have given everything over into the will of God."

36. We also see in this Figure how Jacob commanded them to take the unjust money—that which had been put back into their sacks—and to give it back again. Likewise, a person who wishes to become and be a true Christian must cast away all unrighteousness, everything that he has drawn to himself through craftiness and injustice; that he must give back, at the very least to the poor.

40. A Christian is a new creature in the ground of his heart; his desire is only to do well, not to steal—otherwise, Christ would be a thief within the man. 42. When Christ stood in his suffering, he had nothing but a fine Purple Mantle around him; but when he hung on the Cross, he had it no longer, and even less so in his resurrection. It is valid in penance alone and nowhere else; it is for the poor soul to wrap itself in when it is ashamed of its sins before the Face of God.

59. For Joseph stands in this place as a **Figure of Christ** <note>original: "Figure Christi"; a theological term meaning Joseph’s life acts as a symbolic prophecy of Christ’s life</note>, who has a special food of which they know nothing; just as can be seen at Jacob's well, when his disciples urged him to eat, where he said that he had a food of which they did not know, which was to do the will of the one who had sent him; for the faith of the pagan woman was his special food. <note>A reference to the Woman at the Well in John 4:32-34</note>

61. 62. For faith, in its hungry desire, is the mouth that receives and takes it in; in which grasping or taking in, faith eats and drinks the flesh and blood of Christ. This eating and drinking is enclosed and held within the internal **Paradise-image** <note>A mystical concept describing the original, perfect spiritual form of humanity that was "extinguished" or faded when Adam fell</note>, which faded in Adam and became alive again in Christ. There, the human Paradise-essence and the flesh and blood of Christ are entirely one single essence and remain so eternally. This inner man is then no longer called "Adam," but is named "Christ," being a limb of the Body and essence of Christ. Therein is the Temple of the Holy Spirit, with God's Holy Word dwelling substantially within it; it is a form of the incomprehensible Godhead, being the "imaged Word of God," a true image of God.

63. This imaged Word, or image of God, is now the substantial faith and Christ himself within the person; he who remains in the person and is the life and light of man. That is, the Temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us, as Paul says: "Do you not know that you are temples of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?" <note>1 Corinthians 3:16</note> This same substantial faith is also the branch on the **Vine of Christ**, whose power permeates the entire person, just as the sun permeates a herb.

# Chapter 70. Returning to Egypt to go to Joseph. #

...that such power resides in the life of man, that he could take the essence of God by his own strength—no: it is given to him out of grace. Just as the sun gives itself to the herb by its own will, yet the herb cannot say for that reason, "I am the sun," simply because the sun works within it; in the same way, man cannot say, "I am Christ," because Christ dwells and works in him as in his **Image** <note>Dutch: *Evenbeeld*; a central concept in this theology where man is a reflection or mirror of the divine</note>, or the formed Word of God and the unimaginable Godhead, being the imaged Word of God, a likeness of God.

64. This is precisely the **Figure** <note>A symbolic foreshadowing or type</note> of why *Joseph* was served separately, and his brothers also separately: that there is still a distinction between Christ and his food, and between man and his food. There is no distinction between us and the creaturely humanity of Christ, but there is a distinction regarding the unformed, eternal-speaking Word in him, in which the whole of God is active and birthing—not enclosed, but speaking out in full omnipotence, not as a creature, but as God.

65. Yet in us humans, in so far as man possesses God and Christ within himself as his own essence, the Word is formed and **substantial** <term>Substantial: (Dutch: *wesentlyk*) referring to a spiritual reality that has actual, "weighty" existence rather than being just an abstract thought</term>. And this formed, substantial Word, in turn, eats of the formed Word of God—that is, from the flesh and blood of Christ—where, however, the unformed Word also dwells with the entire fullness of the Godhead.

66. Yet the human creature does not possess this in their own right or ownership, as it is in Christ Jesus, but rather as a vessel and dwelling-place of God on earth. This is like fire possessing iron: the iron becomes entirely fiery, and yet it does not hold the fire by its own power or force; for if the fire is extinguished, the iron remains a dark iron. Or, just as the sun penetrates a plant and grows within the plant and becomes substantial, yet the Spirit of the sun remains only as a power within the plant, and the body of the plant does not become a sun. This is how the relationship between God and man is to be understood.

67. But when *Moses* says that the *Egyptians* were also served separately, because the *Egyptians* were not permitted to eat bread with the *Hebrews*, this also has its **Figure**. Although this may have been the case outwardly—that they did not dare to eat with them, which we leave unchallenged in its own historical value, just like all the rest—we leave it as a history, but we only wish to point out the understanding of why the Spirit of God had it recorded so precisely.

68. When we wish to investigate this, we must consider a natural, **Adamic** <note>Referring to the fallen state of humanity inherited from Adam, characterized by being "natural" rather than "spiritual"</note> man, of whatever lineage or name he may be. All of these may, with a right **Christian**—that is, with the...

## How the Sons of Jacob [behaved] due to the famine, Ch. 70 ##

Joseph’s brothers do not eat; why? They have no mouth for such food, their mouth is still closed to them, and they cannot enjoy the food of the Body of Christ <note>Dutch: *Lig-haams Christi*; Böhme is drawing a parallel between the physical meal in Egypt and the spiritual bread of life</note>; they are an abomination to it, and have a loathing for it, just as one sees that it is a horrible idea to the Jews, Turks <note>In Böhme’s era, "Turks" was the standard term used to refer to Muslims</note>, and Heathens that a Christian says he eats Christ's flesh and drinks his blood.

69. Thus it is currently for nominal Christianity <note>Dutch: *titel-Christenheid*; Böhme’s term for those who are Christian in name only, lacking inner transformation</note>, a thing of horror where one party does not believe in the **substantial** <term>Substantial: (*wesentlyk*) Referring to a spiritual reality that has actual, "weighty" existence rather than being just an abstract thought or metaphor</term> enjoyment of the Body of Christ but wants to take it only spiritually; the other party wants to fill the mouth of the Adamic mortal man and grasp it with the same, and there is no right knowledge or understanding: in neither of those parties. They indeed sit at the table, yet like the ignorant brothers of Joseph, who did not know Joseph; their faith indeed eats, but their understanding does not recognize Joseph in his meal.

70. So now speaks Reason <note>Dutch: *vernuft*; human intellectual capacity operating without divine illumination</note>: since the Jews, Turks, and ignorant Heathens have no mouth for such food; and Christ says, "whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man, has no life in him," then they must all be damned together. O *Israel*! How blind you are here, and know as little as Joseph's brothers knew of Joseph.

71. The Turks, Jews, and foreign peoples, whose desire and prayer <unclear>go</unclear> to the only God, they indeed have a mouth, yet not in the same way as a true Christian. For just as the desire—being the mouth—is, so also is the food in the mouth. They desire the Spirit of God, thus their eating is also like their nature before the incarnation of Christ, in the Father and Son, that is, in the Word.

72. But a true Christian has a true, **substantial** mouth, because the desire of the soul—or much more the substantial Christ, being the Maiden **Sophia** <note>The personification of Divine Wisdom, a central figure in Böhme’s mysticism representing the soul's heavenly counterpart</note>—has a mouth of the substantial Word. But the other [peoples] have a mouth of the insubstantial Word; they desire the property of God the Father, being the only God, and they receive him too, though the grace is not manifest here.

73. But since the Father has given men to his Son Christ, as Christ says, and has revealed the grace in Christ, he offers the same only in Christ, and that outside of Christ there is no salvation; yet He [God] follows him [the seeker] also in the earnest, calling prayer, which Christ takes from his Father and takes into himself, and eats. And he fills them with his humanity, suffering, death, and blood-shedding, and so they are with their spirit **substantially** in Christ, yet in them—that is, in their own self—it is hidden.

74. For they do not desire the flesh of the Son of Man, therefore

Yet, with their spirit, they are substantially <note>Dutch: *wesentlyk*; having a real, spiritual substance or essence</note> in Christ. 75.
